doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The decline of live music and communication
summary: Asked where communicative music is happening today, Davern says synthesizers, a lack of clubs and variety mean the end of music as he loves it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you something else about that. You know music, whereas we know that it’s communication, can also be sonic culture.

And the reason you’re saying something and I want you to elaborate on it a little bit more, and that is, sometimes when I hear an artist, when I hear Louis Armstrong records and when I hear Charlie Parker records, I get the feeling that these players were not just playing something because they had just learned a new scale or learned a new chord, but they were saying something because they really meant it and that was communicating to © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
people who agreed, by their applause and by the enthusiasm in which they accepted these artists.
What, where is that happening today? Are we doing it today or what, if that’s not happening, how can we get it? How can we jump start it?

The tragedy here I think is we are being, we are in the wrong place at the wrong time in the sense that we wouldn’t have this problem if we were born say, for myself 20 years earlier than I was born. You, a great deal more. Because we’re witnessing the end of music as we love it I think. I think physically, one man with a synthesizer can produce four times the amount of volume in a given space, like vis a vis a ballroom, that in 1938 it took 16 men, well trained, practicing bunnies and section rehearsals and okay fellas, to get that kind of intensity and volume into a ballroom, which, because all kids are the same whether it was 1938 or 1998. They all really are morons, you know they really are. But it just so happens the music — that the intensity of the working up, and the pitch of music then, I think was superior to let’s say the same amount of intensity given off in a rock concert. Well actually there’s more intensity given off in a rock concert, but it’s a similar kind of frenzy. Kids need to congregate and do tribal things, you know, tribal rituals, like “The Rite of Spring,” sacrifice of life and stuff. That’s what it all is, it really is. And they have to congregate together and somehow or other, and maybe it’s like some primordial thing where there’s a sense of smell. But the same kids today, as was supposedly back in ‘38 or ‘28 or whenever you talk about them, they’re the same people, the same mentality, and very little has changed as you can tell. But what has changed, and that’s the sad part back to what you asked before, is that the means of communication, vis a vis the instruments, although there are many, many people out there playing instruments, have no place to go with them. And to be usurped by one man and his synthesizer, and there are no more clubs, a few of them but not very many, with a variety of music. That’s the other thing, variety. There’s no variety out there. There’s either very very bad traditional, or very very bad ultra modern, whatever that means, both of which will bore you to tears, even in small doses. So the emotional impact of a single instrumentalist going out there and doing his thing is a rare phenomenon. And I hate to say it, I mean I hate to see it vanish but it’s very possible with the values of the world today as we know it, to see this entire western idea of culture, you know from Bach on to the present day, go bye-bye.
Fall prey to Blockbuster Video and a bag of microwave popcorn?
Sure, that’s right, and a floppy disc. It’s very possible.
